nameStory: The name 'meadow buttercup' comes from its love of open grassy areas and its bright, butter-yellow petals that shine like they've been polished. The 'buttercup' name has a charming folk origin - people would hold the glossy yellow flowers under someone's chin, and if it reflected yellow light on their skin, they supposedly loved butter!
description: Meadow buttercup is a cheerful perennial wildflower that brightens New England fields and meadows from late spring through summer. This upright plant typically grows 1-3 feet tall with deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves and glossy, bright yellow flowers about an inch across. Each flower has five shiny petals that look almost waxy, sitting atop branching stems that give the plant a bushy appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright, glossy yellow flowers with 5 shiny petals that feel waxy to the touch and reflect light like tiny mirrors, typically about 1 inch across

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided leaves cut into 3-7 segments that spread like fingers from a palm, with each segment further toothed or lobed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, branching stems 1-3 feet tall that feel hollow when gently squeezed, growing in clumps from a perennial base

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flattened seed heads that form tight clusters of tiny beaked fruits after flowers fade

habitat: Look for meadow buttercup in open, sunny areas like fields, meadows, pastures, and roadside ditches throughout New England. It thrives in moist, fertile soils and is often found alongside other common meadow flowers like daisies and clovers. This European native has naturalized so well here that it's become a signature flower of New England's rural landscape.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as deeply divided rosettes close to the ground, with flowering stems beginning to develop in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from late May through August, with the brightest, glossiest yellow flowers appearing in early to mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed heads mature, while basal leaves may remain green well into autumn before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to underground roots, leaving no visible trace above ground until spring growth resumes.

funFact: All buttercups contain a toxic compound called ranunculin that makes them taste so terrible that even hungry cows avoid them - which is why you'll often see buttercups thriving in heavily grazed pastures where most other wildflowers have been eaten!
confusionNotes: Meadow buttercup is most easily confused with creeping buttercup, but creeping buttercup spreads by runners along the ground and has three-part leaves (not the deeply divided palm-like leaves of meadow buttercup). Memory trick: meadow buttercup 'reaches up' tall in meadows, while creeping buttercup 'creeps along' the ground.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'meadow' plant, this species is actually native to Europe and was introduced to North America, where it has become so common that many people assume it's a native wildflower. The genus name Ranunculus means 'little frog' in Latin, referring to how many buttercup species love wet, marshy places where frogs live.
compareHints: Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves. Creeping buttercup has three-part leaves and spreads by runners, while bulbous buttercup has a swollen stem base and hairy, less-divided leaves. Small-flowered buttercup has tiny, inconspicuous yellow flowers much smaller than meadow buttercup's showy inch-wide blooms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
